Vehicles commute amid a layer of smog around IGI Airport as the Air Quality Index (AQI) reaches 351, categorised as 'Very Poor' according to the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), in New Delhi on Saturday. (ANI Video Grab) | Photo Credit: ANI
Air quality remained in the ‘poor’ to ‘very poor’ categories across Delhi-NCR on Saturday, with Delhi recording a 24-hour average Air Quality Index (AQI) of 367. The AQI had touched the ‘severe’ category at 403 on Friday morning before settling at 373 by 4 p.m.
Some relief may be in sight, with light rain forecast for Sunday, according to the Air Quality Early Warning System (AQEWS) for Delhi and the India Meteorological Department (IMD).
“A Western Disturbance is likely to cause light/moderate rainfall/snowfall over the Western Himalayan Region and light rainfall over the plains of Northwest India on November 15,” the IMD forecast said.
Of the 59 monitoring stations that recorded data on Saturday, 17 reported ‘severe’ air quality, 38 ‘very poor’, three ‘poor’ and one ‘moderate’. The city’s average AQI improved marginally from 373 on Friday to 367 on Saturday.
According to the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), an AQI between zero and 50 is classified as ‘good’, 51 and 100 as ‘satisfactory’, 101 and 200 as ‘moderate’, 201 and 300 as ‘poor’, 301 and 400 as ‘very poor’, and 401 and 500 as ‘severe’.
The transport sector was the largest contributor to Delhi’s pollution on Saturday, accounting for 20.5%, according to the Decision Support System (DSS). Stubble burning contributed 13.3%. Satellite data recorded 537 farm-fire incidents across six States on Saturday.
Of these, 214 incidents were reported in Punjab, 11 in Haryana, 33 in Uttar Pradesh, 33 in Rajasthan and 246 in Madhya Pradesh.
A total of 11,342 farm-fire incidents were detected across these States between September 15 and November 13, according to a bulletin issued by the Consortium for Research on Agroecosystem Monitoring and Modelling from Space (CREAMS) Laboratory of the Indian Agricultural Research Institute.
Meanwhile, in Gurugram, the administration will install 300 Automated Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) cameras at petrol pumps in the first phase, beginning November 15, to enforce the ‘no valid pollution under control (PUC) certificate, no fuel’ policy. The cameras will read vehicle number plates and cross-check registration details against online PUC records, District Transport Officer and Secretary of the Regional Transport Authority Sanjeev Singla said. Petrol pumps have also been directed to display warning boards stating that vehicles without valid PUC certificates will not be provided fuel.
Ghaziabad has again figured among the five most polluted districts in the country for three consecutive days. Its AQI stood at 338 on November 12, 368 on November 13 and 352 on November 14, making it the fifth, third and fourth most polluted district on the respective days. Residents raised concerns over pollution-control measures, alleging that garbage heaps and roadside soil excavated for pipeline work were adding to pollution in areas including Vasundhara and Indirapuram.
The Uttar Pradesh Pollution Control Board said it had received complaints about violations of GRAP-III restrictions and taken action. The district administration has also directed schools to conduct classes for students from nursery to Class 5 in hybrid mode.
